#6245. At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

Our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

When it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

Many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

For those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

If 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, said. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

#6244. How I Travel: Audra McDonald Needs a Humidifier in Her Hotel Room

Theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history. So what elixirs, potions, and special teas does she keep with her to ensure the quality of her voice as she travels the world to sing? “I mask up on planes. I’m traveling all over the country to do concerts; I can’t land and be sick,” she says. “And I try to make sure there's a humidifier in the hotel room. Those are the two main things.”

While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is currently airing on HBO. She spoke with Condé Nast Traveler from Australia, where her husband Will Swenson is currently starring in the Oz production of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical, about traveling with their 10-year-old daughter, the unspeakable glories of New Zealand, and why you simply can’t top New York City in the final months of the year.

I don't think you can beat New York City. I've lived there for 36 years and it's always such a beautiful time. We have dear friends with a kid around my youngest child's age, and we've been going to the holiday spectacular at Radio City. My sister makes sure that she takes my daughters to The Nutcracker every year at City Ballet. We always try to go see the tree at Rockefeller Center. The one day I don't like in New York City during the holidays is Santa Con, but other than that, I'm down.

Her favorite venue on Earth in which to perform:

There's something about Carnegie Hall [in Manhattan] that is magic. I last sang at Carnegie Hall about six, seven months ago—I'm on the board there now, as well—and the nerves I normally get [before a performance] are always tenfold when I'm getting ready there.

Then the minute I step out on that stage, the hall just gives you a hug that says, You're here to do what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to make music, you're supposed to celebrate music, you're supposed to commune with your audience, and glorious sounds are supposed to be heard. Carnegie Hall is built for all the sound to be glorious. That [venue] takes care of me.

Don't worry about how they act up on a plane. Do what you can, but it's not the flight attendants’ first time at the rodeo. You're never going to see any of these other people again. When we flew out to Australia, my daughter got some weird stomach bug that started the minute they shut the door, and she vomited for the first eight hours of that 15-hour flight. The flight attendants just kept bringing bags and stuff and were like… [mimes a blasé hand gesture]. There was nothing we could do! We were over the ocean. I was giving myself grace. I was giving my poor daughter grace. I just wanted her to feel better, and I was doing the best I could. That’s what I would say to other parents. They’ve seen it all, so don’t worry about what other people are thinking. Everybody has headphones now! We’re fine!

I am not preparing for work! That's the ADHD in me. I am also not sleeping because I cannot sleep on planes very well, unless I'm really knocked out with the help of sleeping pills or something, and I don't like to do that. I try to watch movies, but I'm not good at it, either. My dad was killed in a plane crash about 20 years ago, so normally what I'm doing on a plane—when I'm not taking care of my daughter vomiting—is watching the flight path and seeing where we are in the sky. Then, if there's Wi-Fi, I check to see the weather ahead. Like I'm helping! I don't know what I'm doing, but it calms me down to be like, “Okay, I see that there is weather up ahead, so I should expect that it's probably going to be bumpy.” I don't know if in my mind, I'm thinking [as if] I can warn the pilot. I’ve got to go to therapy, but that's what I do on a plane.

New Zealand, holy wow. My husband and I were asked to sing on a Playbill cruise in Tahiti. We flew to Tahiti with our two daughters, and then I had three and a half weeks off before I started my Australian tour, so we went to New Zealand. I'm going to get emotional talking about it. Every place we visited—the North Island, the South Island, Queenstown, Rotorua, Hahei Beach, the Southern Alps, Christchurch, Wellington—all of it was just one wow after another. The people were lovely. We went to Hobbiton. We drove everywhere, and every second of it was mind-blowing. We even did the mailboat, where you go with this guy on a boat to deliver the mail in an area you can only access by water. I want to go back!

The destination she swears she loved before everyone else:

When we first start going, I wasn’t hearing about a lot of people there, but now everybody goes to Portugal. We have friends who live there, so we started visiting a lot, and not just Lisbon or the Algarve or Porto, though we love Porto. It was also the beautiful countryside and hills and tiny little villages. The topography there is stunning. It’s getting more expensive now, but we used to get incredible bottles of wine for €3! In fact, we have a farm there now, we love it so much.

Toothbrush and toothpaste. Not every hotel provides that, and I just love it when they do. If they've got a toothbrush and toothpaste in there, they've probably gotten a lot of the other amenities right too.

The farthest flung place she’s ever been recognized:

Here in Australia. I was in the South Melbourne neighborhood we've been living in, and I went into a little bookstore near my daughter's school, and someone recognized me. They said, “Were you the one who recorded Emily Wilson's translation of The Iliad book on tape? I loved your work in that.” And I was like, “Whoa, what? Yes I did, wow, thank you.” Doing The Iliad on tape almost killed me. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, so the fact that she wanted to thank me for it? I don’t think my mom knows I did that!

I really want to take a trip to Africa. Obviously, I want to go to Ghana and see where our journey started. I want to go to Kenya and do a safari. I want to go on a trek to see the gorillas. I've been to Egypt, to Cairo, but that's the only time I've been to Africa. I want to wait a couple more years, until my daughter's about 13, and then I will take her. That's going to be our trip.

#6243. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6241. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6240. Delta Air Lines Cuts JFK–Dulles Route After More Than 30 Years

Delta Air Lines will end nonstop service between Washington Dulles and New York JFK in February, leaving the two airports without a direct link. The cut removes another connection to Delta’s JFK hub and follows similar exits by United and JetBlue.

Delta will operate its final flight between Washington Dulles (IAD) and New York Kennedy (JFK) on February 10, 2027. The move eliminates the only nonstop link between the two airports (JetBlue cut the route in 2019 and United in 2014). Delta is not leaving Dulles, nor will this route cut eliminate flights between Dulles and the New York metropolitan area. United serves Newark and LaGuardia from its Washington hub.

But passengers who specifically want to connect at JFK on Delta or its partners will lose an option.

This route has run for over 30 years, so the route cut is certainly newsworthy. Without seeing Delta’s route economics, I’m not going to speculate how much money this service made or lost. But I struggle to see a large number of passengers who need this particular connection and cannot reasonably be accommodated elsewhere. I’m frankly surprised Delta operated a route like this for so long, which sounds like the sort of slot-squatting United does by scheulding so many flights between Washington National and Newark.

The case for this route has always been onward connections at JFK, particularly to international flights. But even there, Delta has alternatives. Washington-area passengers can begin at Reagan National (DCA), while travelers who prefer Dulles can connect through another Delta hub, such as Atlanta or Detroit, depending on their destination. I cannot imagine that there is so connecting traffic from Northern Virginia and the broader Washington area that Delta cannot handle it through DCA or another hub.

While I’m sure there will be “regulars” who are greatly inconvenienced by this route cut, that’s no justification to keep any route going and we do know the load factor was lower on this route than its network average.

This brought back memories of my coverage of United ending JFK–Dulles service in October 2014.

“Two-thirds of traffic on the route is connecting traffic that does not generate sufficient yields.”

United’s circumstances were somewhat similar. Dulles was its hub, while JFK had become a small station focused on flights to Los Angeles and San Francisco. Today, Delta operates a substantial hub at JFK, but it only flies to its hubs, now less JFK, from IAD.

In both cases the underlying question is similar: does the connecting revenue justify using an aircraft and scarce airport access on a short route when passengers have other ways to reach the network?

United decided it did not. Delta is now removing the same airport pair from its schedule.

More than 12 years later, I still find United’s explanation brutally honest as to why it cut that route (and eventually pulled out of JFK altogether).

I have written about Delta becoming more selective at JFK, including cuts to domestic feeder routes and international destinations. With air traffic control congestion and slot restrictions still in place, it makes sense to me that Delta would want to funnel less travel through JFK and more throughout other hubs: the focus must be on local traffic or at least costal traffic that can command a higher premium.

Meanwhile, United is preparing to return to JFK through its partnership with JetBlue. Does this create an opening for United to restore Dulles service? Perhaps, but I would think it would be difficult to work now just like it was then and has been for Delta. United already has extensive Washington–New York connectivity through Newark, and its initial JFK access will be limited. Each available slot will have more compelling uses via transcon traffic.

I do not think the disappearance of Delta from this route will make starting that route attractive to United, especially since United previously abandoned it.

Delta will end JFK–Dulles flights after February 10, 2027, removing a useful option for some Washington-area passengers connecting through Kennedy. Even so, the decision makes sense to me. Delta can accommodate much of that traffic through Reagan National or other hubs, and local Washington–New York travelers have several alternatives…so no, this isn’t a sign that Delta is continuing to lose ground in New York.

United cut this route in 2014 because connecting traffic did not produce sufficient revenue. Delta has not publicly supplied the same explanation, but the commercial question remains much the same. A “useful connection” for many passengers does not necessarily mean a profitable or smart one for the airline.

#6239. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6238. Aer Lingus Unveils Business Class Suites With Doors And Its First Premium Economy Cabin On A330s

Aer Lingus has announced a cabin overhaul for 10 Airbus A330 aircraft, with the first refurbished jet scheduled to enter service on October 1, 2027. The initial route will be Dublin–New York JFK, on select EI104/EI105 services. Additional North American routes will follow as more aircraft are refurbished.

This is an A330-only project for now: there will be no corresponding cabin overhaul for the Airbus A321LR or A321XLR.

The refurbished aircraft will feature 28 Collins Elevation business class suites in a 1-2-1 layout. Every passenger will have direct aisle access and a closing door, with each seat converting into a 78-inch flat bed. Improved bedding and amenity kits are also planned.

The renderings look attractive to me. Green upholstery and lighter finishes give the cabin an Irish identity and a premium feel (hello Singapore Airlines). More importantly, the layout addresses a weakness I encountered on my Aer Lingus A330-200 flight from Dublin to Los Angeles. I had a window seat with a passenger beside me and no direct aisle access. Storage was limited too.

I slept well, but the seat was behind what many competitors offered. The lovely crew helped redeem that flight, though warm service should complement a competitive seat rather than compensate for one. Doors are fine, but giving every passenger access to the aisle is the more consequential improvement.

Aer Lingus also plans refreshed dining and a self-service business class snack and refreshment bar, much like SAS offers its on its A330 aircraft:

The new premium economy cabin will have four rows of Recaro R4 seats:

Passengers will receive an upgraded three-course meal, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones. It’s a hardly a unique or transformative hard product compared to its peers, but it’s an increasingly important middle way providing a noticeably more comfortable seat at a price that makes sense relative to economy and business class.

This fills an obvious gap for Aer Lingus. Someone who wants more room than economy offers but cannot justify a business class fare currently has limited options within the airline’s own cabin lineup. A genuine premium economy product gives that passenger another reason to stay with Aer Lingus.

Economy will retain the A330’s appealing 2-4-2 layout, with new seats and adjustable headrests. A self-service snack station is coming to this cabin too.

If I fly economy class, I prefer the A330 or 767. Two seats together by the window remain a compelling reason to choose an A330 when traveling as a couple, especially compared with being part of a block of three on most other widebody aircraft.

Aer Lingus promises more personal space, but we will wait for the final seat pitch and total economy seat count before drawing conclusions about legroom. A redesigned seatback can improve knee clearance without increasing the distance between rows, but padding is also essential.

The refurbished A330s will receive Panasonic Astrova entertainment systems, with 4K screens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and USB-C charging.

Free Starlink Wi-Fi will also be available, though Aer Lingus says that service is already offered across its transatlantic routes. Passengers do not need to wait for the new cabins to benefit from it. My previous A330 flight featured an entertainment system with missing graphics and internet that was slow but stable. Working screens and fast connectivity would improve the experience considerably.

For a daytime transatlantic flight, I place enormous value on reliable internet. A better seat may help me sleep on the overnight journey to Dublin, but Starlink makes the flight home a far more useful part of my day.

The first aircraft is still almost a year away, and the announcement does not provide a completion date for all 10 retrofits.

An October 1 launch on select JFK flights should not be confused with every Aer Lingus A330 having the new cabins from that date, even to JFK. During the transition, you’ll be able to tell which aircraft have the new business class because that aircraft will also be selling premium economy seats.

I hope Aer Lingus makes the differences clear during booking and handles aircraft substitutions sensibly…

Aer Lingus is giving 10 A330s new business class suites, adding premium economy, and refreshing economy class, with the first aircraft scheduled to debut between Dublin and New York JFK in October 2027.

My last longhaul flight on Aer Lingus left me impressed by the crew but disappointed by parts of the onboard product. This overhaul addresses the seat and technology shortcomings that made me reluctant to seek out the airline. I look forward to trying it. Aer Lingus already showed me how pleasant its service can be. Pair that with a competitive seat and better catering, and I might go out of my way to book it again.

#6237. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6236. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6235. Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

World of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

Hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

Globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

Hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

“This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”

After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

The ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

That addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to plan a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

For someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

There are still restrictions. For example, the new Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

Some milestone free night certificates currently expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very quickly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

But Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards currently can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

Here are some notable new choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):

The $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

At 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking…

The new Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice new update.

The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

But the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

The reality is that aspirational properties, the ones a Globalist would likely be wanting to use points at (I hope!) are rarely going to result in the need for parking. I do feel bad for you that you got a concierge that is less than helpful, but it’s not the case across the board. I have had two over the past ten years and both have been amazing. They respond by email during working hours in minutes and have handled some unusual requests for me just wonderfully. I guess my point being that if it’s so bad with yours (and I know Ben says the same on OMAAT about his) I’m at a loss at why you don’t start sending out emails as such to get a new one assigned. Or talk to your concierge directly and express your thoughts as to why you are unhappy – with a focus to help them help you better.

I had a new one assigned. It still takes 36 hours to get replies. When I call, I never get that person. I get a general globalist concierge agent. The only good the agents have done is correct points that didn’t post correctly.

Mine were all horrible too, but I have heard of some great ones…

I personally wish they’d get rid of the club passes since it seems that most properties I’ve been to sinve covid have closed them. I’d prefer free breakfast vouchers for the years I come up short of globalist.

I think the club lounge passes or certificates — whatever they are called — are a complete scam since the vast majority of Hyatt Regency and Grand Hyatt properties, at least in the United States, no longer have an open or operational club lounge.

It would be nice if they were Club Access and/or Free Breakfast certificates…

#6234. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

Actually – just looked up what I read and I think it’s the $250 credit every six months that requires a 2-night stay but not the other benefits. So looks like you could have spent 12,500 points + $250 cash for a second night and gotten the $250 credited back.

#6233. Review: Austrian Airlines A320 Economy Class

After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.

We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.

The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.

Stepping onboard, we headed to the back to find our seats in row 22.

The Austrian A320 has 180 seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration (same in business class, though the middle seat is blocked).

The Recaro BL3520 “NEK” slimline seats are very uncomfortable with very little padding. These are familiar seats if you have flown within Europe on Lufthansa Group carriers, with a literature pocket and a folding tray table on the seatback ahead.

Legroom varies by aircraft and row. Austrian lists a minimum economy class seat pitch of just 28 inches across its A320 fleet, so do not expect much room to stretch out, though it felt like we had 29 inches.

There are no power ports or USB ports on this aircraft. Thankfully, however, there are individual air vents, unlike on the 777.

In economy class, passengers receive a free glass of water and Austrian chocolate.

For those peckish, buy-on-board is available. I pre-ordered a hot meal from the carrier’s Austrian Melangerie menu.

What else would I order on Austrian Airlines but Wiener Schnitzel? While a proper Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal, Austrian uses chicken onboard, describing the dish as:

Golden-brown chicken schnitzel with parsley potatoes

The price was €13.80, though I received a 10% discount for pre-ordering.

Presentation was very much like economy class: the schnitzel and potatoes were served together in a cardboard box, but sometimes you have to look beyond the presentation. The chicken was tender, the breading remained surprisingly crisp, and the parsley potatoes were a nice accompaniment…my son Augustine and I both enjoyed it.

I highlighted this meal in a recent Meal of the Week feature.

> Read More: Austrian Airlines’ €13.80 Wiener Schnitzel On An 80-Minute Flight

I had also hoped to try the Julius Meinl Wiener Melange, a €5.20 coffee served with milk foam in a proper ceramic cup on a silver tray. Alas, Austrian only offers the Melange on flights of at least 80 minutes and our Vienna to Zürich flight was apparently five minutes too short according to the flight attendant.

Before landing I used the lavatory in the rear of the aircraft and it was messy by that point, with paper towels overflowing from the waste receptacle.

While there is no seatback screens or streaming movies and TV shows, Wi-Fi was available for purchase onboard. A high speed pass (Viasat) was 6€ while messaging was free. I had trouble connecting, initially, but ultimately was able to pay the 6€ and connect.

This was a quick, boring flight with a delicious lunch onboard thanks to the buy-on-board menu. I’d never go out of my way to fly Austrian shorthaul in economy class, but if you are stuck behind the curtain, do take advantage of the pre-order menu to make the flight go by a bit faster.

My original review, covering an Austrian Airlines A320 journey from Vienna to Yerevan, Armenian (fun trip!) in 2019 is below.

What is Austrian Airlines like on a mid-haul flight in economy class?

My business partner, John, and I spent a weekend in Yerevan, Armenia last month. We were in Vienna earlier in the week, so the nonstop Austrian flight from VIE to EVN made the most sense. We booked for 15,000 United miles each in economy class.

Business class would have been an extra 10,000 miles, but I figured 1.) the seat is the same, 2.) I already had lounge access, and 3.) we would be eating dinner just before the flight. So the upgrade did not make sense.

Vienna International Airport is such an easy airport to navigate. Check-in (John had to check a bag), security, and passport control took only a few moments. I’ll review the Austrian lounge in a separate post.

Boarding commenced precisely on schedule with business class passenger and Star Alliance Gold members invited to board first.

I’ll start with the seats and the following warning: these slimline seats are very uncomfortable. By the time we reached Yerevan three hours later, I could not wait to get off. The seats do recline slightly, but the lack of padding makes for an uncomfortable flying experience on flights longer than 60-90 minutes. But that’s hardly a unique experience to Austrian. Seat pitch is 30 inches.

Notice that the only difference in business class hard product is that the middle seat is blocked:

A sticker on the aircraft fuselage indicated wi-fi internet would be available, but it did not function. There are no in-seat power ports.

First, I appreciated the pillows and blankets, both of which were better than many airlines offer in economy class. Heck, United does not even offer pillows in domestic first class except on premium transcontinental flight.

That said, it was roasting outside and the cabin was not overly cool…not exactly heavy blanket weather.

Second, I appreciated the meal, as small as it was. A vegetarian cheese pasta with cake and bread was served after takeoff. Talk about a load of carbs! Passengers were not offered a choice of meal.

Flight attendants came around before the meal and also about 90 minutes before landing with a beverage serevice.

Finally, the lavatory was very clean…these pictures are toward the end of the flight.

I appreciate that Austrian is full service in the sense that blankets, pillows, and meals are provided. But three hours really pushes the limit for this type of slimline seat. I’ll happily fly Austrian again, but ideally on a shorthaul route or on a widebody jet in business class…

> Review: Austrian Airlines 767 Business Class from Beijing to Vienna

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

I have never understood who pays for the business class when it is the same seat, and if you have status you can get within a few rows of the front of the plane in economy.

I also don’t understand why all EU countries fly planes with no real business/first on flights that are this long, (2-4 hours) and are very much international. Almost all US planes have domestic first, even if they are only going an hour or two. How did things evolve so differently in the EU??

Many executives in Europe have business class travel as a part of their contracts. Non-cash perks like company cars, per diems, and travel perks are (and have historically been) more common there because they’re not taxed the same way (if at all) as wage/salary income.

These flex systems, although offering an inferior hard product, allow European carriers to flex their cabins to accommodate far more business class fliers. I’ve seen as many as the first 12 rows flexed to biz!

@Lara S, mallthus is correct that the present business class model allows for flexibility depending upon loads. Aeroflot, Tarom, and Turkish have real business class seats.

Iberia has also started incorporating ‘real’ business class seats on short to mid-haul flights on its A319..I had it from MAD-FLR, but I think its more commonly used on routes to Tel Aviv, Moscow Etc.

Looks and reminds me a lot of DLs old J seat on their 767s..

One reason to use it is when connecting with a long haul flight. Suppose you buy a business class ticket from New York to Yerevan via Vienna. You’d get the real thing in the trans Atlantic section, then a blocked middle seat.

The seats are the same as LH. After two hours on one recently I had back pain and a numb a*se. Apparently they are now being replaced by ones that according to the LH CEO Spohr are ‘even more comfortable’. I wait in fear!

Austrian unlike the other LH group carriers also use these seats on their long haul aircraft in economy. You have been warned!

I think Europeans find US Domestic premium cabins and products as strange and confusing as we find their intro-European premium product.

In the US, we call it First Class (but it’s closer to Business Class). You get a big seat with more leg room. Generally the plane is WiFi equipped with either IFE or streaming entertainment at no charge. You only get a meal if it’s over a certain length (2-3 hours) and during meal times. You also do not get Lounge access (but lounge access is commonly available through a credit card or membership program).

In the EU, you get a coach seat with a blocked middle. The leg room is less than what is available in the US in the Economy Plus, Main Cabin Extra, etc. cabins. You get Lounge access and a meal that is generally better than what you would get on a US carrier for the same stage length. WiFi and IFE/streaming entertainment is not as common.

I absolutely prefer the US model but it is what I am used to. I get my Lounge access through my credit cards. I would prefer an MCE seat to Euro Business any day and I can book those seats at ticketing. But I’m guessing some Euro business man would find the lack of a meal and complimentary lounge access disappointing.

FOLKS, note this is a brand new review that I just stacked on top of my old one.

#6232. JSX Adds New Route From NY

JSX is launching a new nonstop route between the New York metro area and North Texas.

Starting Feb. 17, the public charter service will connect Teterboro Airport in New Jersey with Dallas Love Field. Flights will operate daily.

The service will be available only to members of the carrier’s free loyalty program, Club JSX.

“New York City and Dallas are two of America’s most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a news release. “As we continue expanding our network, our focus remains on giving customers something increasingly rare in air travel: more of their time back. With this new daily service, we’re bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country’s most important travel corridors.”

JSX added service to Teterboro, which it markets as New York City, in 2025. It also serves Westchester County Airport, located just north of New York.
