#6197. On Tour: Australian Indie Darling Radio Free Alice on Tour Life, Guerrilla Gigs, and American Motels

This article is part of a new series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.

On Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in New York City's Tompkins Square Park. They were there for a quintessentially East Village pop-up concert headlined by the Melbourne-based post-punk band Radio Free Alice (followed by an after party at Niagara). The band's debut album, What’s In Between, was just released the day prior, blending the high energy of ’80s new wave with biting social satire and a healthy dose of cheek. Having picked up a following in Australia and Europe, the four-piece group has built an underground reputation on guerrilla gigs like this one—held everywhere from beneath London railway bridges and Melbourne’s former Pentridge Prison to suburban backyards in Austin, Texas.

That’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home. They’re in the thick of their own coming-of-age story, and one that's unfolding on an international stage. Fresh off the first dates of a nearly sold-out European lineup, tickets are now on sale for their What's In Between North America tour, which will kick off in San Francisco on February 24, 2027.

Earlier this month, vocalist and guitarist Noah Learmonth picked up my call from a Sprinter van somewhere in Germany, on the road from Copenhagen to Berlin. With the wit, gumption, and on-stage vocals of a Gen-Z Morrissey, his devilish grin fills the screen as he tells me he spends 99% of his time in the window seat behind the van’s little table, facing forward. His preferred seat is currently occupied by guitarist Jules Paradiso. He gives me a 360-degree tour of their ecosystem, where everyone has settled into their own version of life on the road. Drummer Lochie Dowd has claimed a small sleeping nook near the back. Michael Phillips, bassist and resident reader, sits with his Kindle, having just finished Christos Tsiolkas’s The Slap. As for who’s running the show? “Fuck, no one,” the still-grinning Noah says. “There’s a man up front called Ben, our tour manager, who’s a crazy man. He’s the one who leads the blind. We’d all be fucked otherwise.”

What’s everyone’s travel personality on tour? Who’s running the show?

Yeah, [I'm] type D. I’m sort of in my own world when I’m traveling—headphones on, that kind of vibe. Jules is really easy company. He’s a valuable asset to have in the world. Michael’s pretty chill, too. He’s looking at me now as I summarize his personality. Lochie likes to sleep in this little nook. That’s a big part of his tour experience: finding that little nook.

When we met Ben, we just fell in love with him and his crazy methods, his madness. The thing about Ben is he gets our sound right every time. It’s really annoying when someone else does the sound and you watch the videos back and go, ‘Oh my God, what the fuck? Why is there no bass in the synth? Why do we sound like Duran Duran? What’s going on? I sound like Sonic Youth.’ That’s not at all what we were going for. Two of my favorite bands, though. But Ben gets exactly the sound we’re going for, and he’s a real empath. We’ve spent so much time on the road together. He’s our guy.

Where do you stay while you're on the road?

When we’re touring Europe, we’ll stay in budget hotels. Either an Ibis or a Travelodge. In America, it’s more motel-type places—Motel 6 kind of things. It’s very cliché, but kind of sick in a way. Each morning when you wake up, you set your alarm for half an hour before you have to leave, get up, have a shower, smash your clothes into your backpack, and run down to the lobby so you’re not late and Ben doesn’t give you a verbal spanking.

Terrible. I just had McDonald’s. I don’t even like McDonald’s. You literally don’t have an option. You pull into a service station and the only food there is McDonald’s. Jules is a Big Mac guy, though. I know that.

I’m personally notoriously light. I just have this yellow North Face backpack that I’ve had since I was about seven years old. My auntie gave it to me for my birthday. My trusty yellow backpack. Lochie has a big suitcase, Michael has a smaller suitcase, and Jules has a big, backpacker-style backpack.

I’m wearing the same jeans I’ve been wearing every day for the past year. I got them from a thrift shop in Melbourne. So my essentials are my jeans. Lochie’s are his headphones—we all use Sony. Jules’s is…video games. He’d hate that I just said that. Let’s say his laptop. Michael’s is his Kindle. He’s the best reader. Let’s see what he’s reading…ah, he just finished The Slap.

What's your favorite city that you've played in so far?

New York. I mean, the obvious answer is New York. New York’s the best city in the fucking world. It’s amazing.

The first few times we were there, we partied a lot. We just said, ‘This is a fucking adult amusement park.’ It’s ridiculous. We were staying with this band called Been Stellar, too, who are great. When we’re back we like going out on the Lower East Side, especially to this bar called Treasure Club. I personally also love the diners. I think the atmosphere in an old-school, family-run diner might be the best atmosphere of any place in the world.

A gig is just people playing music, and it can happen literally anywhere. There are no rules. You can do it anywhere. Shaking up the gig setting—rethinking what a gig is and what it can feel like—is really fun, and it keeps it important. The Melbourne set at Pentridge Prison [a former 19th century prison that's been transformed into a residential area] was sick. It was an incredible visual.

Zurich. So random. I just remember having a strangely amazing time. I remember leaving that gig thinking, ‘Actually, there was something incredibly awesome and sweet about that.’ And it was the people. They were just these thoughtful, sweet people.

After a show like Zurich, we’ll be in the green room after. We’ll probably crack open a beer, and Lochie will be funny. If it went really, really well, we might go out somewhere nearby, to a pub or a bar or something. But generally, what happens is we go back to the green room, we’re really buzzed, we’ll have a beer and we’ll be pretty hyped up. Then Ben will come in and say, ‘All hands on deck. We need to load up the van. We’ve got to get to the next city.’ Zurich, though—I’d love to do it again.

What's your impression of the United States so far?

I mean, there’s one thing about America: the difference between, say, New York and LA, and then LA and Minneapolis or somewhere, is worlds apart. You could be in completely different countries.

Middle America can feel like an absolute time warp. When you’re on the road, there’s a sort of repetitiveness to the long stretches of road that all seem to look exactly the same. You arrive at a petrol station that’s identical to the last one you stopped at. There’s that stereotype that Americans are big talkers, but I’ve found that’s almost underrated. I can’t believe how chatty Americans are. They love just talking, going on and on. Coming from Australia, it’s the opposite. I love it.

Any memories you've made on the road that you’ll never forget?

The first time we played in LA, this very sweet girl called Alice randomly made us all these gifts. She gave us all these handmade things: embroidered bracelets with band-related names and glasses with our names on them. I find something quite American about that. It’s just so sweet. In Europe, people tend to be a little less expressive in that way. It’s still just amazing to me.

Glasgow had this sort of “rara”-ness to it, which was really fun and funny for us. It just felt so boisterous. We’d play a slower song, and they’d still find a way to just absolutely lose their minds. It was cute.

When you're not on tour, where’s home for you guys?

Nowhere, not really anywhere. I’m not exaggerating. I feel disingenuous calling anywhere our home at this point. But if there were one, it would be London. It’s making a big impression on us. What’s cool is that, a year before we moved to London, we played to maybe one person at one of our gigs there. Then, the following year, we played to this really big, sold-out room. It was an incredibly high-energy, adrenaline-fueled, amazing, crazy show. That was special. I’ll never forget it. It was probably my favorite show.

There are so many young indie-rock bands coming up in London that I’m seeing, and they’re all ambitious and exciting. I’m really excited by London. It’s lived up to the hopes I had for it. Because of that we’ve found ourselves hanging out at venues like the Shacklewell Arms and the George Tavern, that sort of thing.

While you're on tour, what do you miss the most?

You know, this isn’t a very cool answer, and I kind of wish it were, but the truth is I really miss having an exercise routine. In Melbourne, I was really big on swimming every morning, doing laps or going to the gym. I find it puts me in a really good place for the day. I’m chill and focused, not neurotic, and I just find it’s really good for me.

What's a band touring right now that you are personally excited about?

Lime Garden. They’re an all female lineup. The English rock scene is a bit of a sausage fest, so they’re a breath of fresh air.

#6196. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6194. I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right big toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip.

I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding new sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary.

Since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast.

A view of the South West coast Path's rugged countryside, which is now more easily accessible to hikers thanks to the wider newly created King Charles III England Coast Path.

When I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago.

By setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night.

After 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower.

A view of Durdle Door, a limestone arch that can be seen from the trail

My second day of walking presented a new challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.”

But thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun.

Perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered.

A solo walker making their way along the South West Coast Path

I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble.

When I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy.

The final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed.

Boats bob in the water near Old Harry Rocks in Studland, Dorset

The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat.

On the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

#6193. Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez says.

Among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

When they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez Álvarez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

“Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez says. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”

Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

At the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez says.

Be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” quickly ferries over their order.

Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

Azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”

She didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she says. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

Other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado

The married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Fossa says. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

Their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, New York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and New York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

Back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”

There are six United credit cards, ranging from a no-annual-fee card to premium personal and business cards with United Club access. Fortunately, figuring out which ones you're eligible for is straightforward.

Holding one United card generally doesn't prevent you from opening another or earning its welcome bonus. Instead, welcome-offer restrictions are largely card-specific: You can’t apply for a card you already hold or earn its welcome bonus if you've received a bonus on that same card in the last 24 months.

For United cards, applicants need to clear three main hurdles:

Meeting these requirements doesn't guarantee approval, only that you are free to apply and are eligible for the welcome offer if approved.

Chase allows you to apply for multiple United cards, as long as they are separate cards.

For example, if you already hold an , you can also apply for a . However, you can't hold two of the same card, so if you have a Quest card, you can't get a second in order to double up on its benefits.

The Gateway, Explorer, Quest and Club offer different benefits, so holding more than one could make sense depending on your travel habits. Having two or more cards means you also have access to different bonus categories when earning miles and potentially multiple PQP deposits for being a cardholder, depending on which cards you have.

There's one exception: If you are an existing United Club Visa Signature cardmember (no longer available to new applicants), you are not eligible for the current United Club card.

You'll need to close the old card and apply for a new Club card 24 months after you received the initial bonus. Or, you can call the number on the back of your card to product change to the current Club card, which preserves your account history and 5/24 status but won't earn an introductory offer.

You won't qualify if you currently hold the business card you're applying for or received its new-cardmember bonus within the past 24 months.

You don't need an LLC or a company with employees to apply. You may qualify with a legitimate sole proprietorship or side hustle, such as freelance work, consulting, pet sitting or reselling.

Chase generally requires business card applicants to be under 5/24. However, once you're approved, a Chase business card typically won't appear on your personal credit report or add another account to your 5/24 total.

Yes, you can have multiple United credit cards at one time. Unlike some other airline credit cards, United's cards don't have a broad restriction that prevents you from holding multiple cobranded cards.

You could hold a for its TravelBank Cash and 10,000-mile award discount, the for lounge access and a for business expenses.

There's also an incentive to pair a personal and business United card: Both United business cards offer 5,000 bonus miles each account anniversary if you're also the primary cardmember on a personal United card.

Holding multiple United cards won't make sense for infrequent flyers, since benefits like free checked bags and priority boarding overlap on multiple cards. However, for loyal customers, the collection of slightly different perks and cardholder PQP bonuses could justify the cost of paying multiple annual fees.

Yes, you can get the same United credit card more than once. However, you will only earn another welcome offer if you no longer hold that card and at least 24 months have passed since you received the new-cardmember bonus.

Remember, Chase counts from the date you receive the bonus, not from when you open or close the account.

If you are an authorized user on someone else's United card, Chase does not consider that being a current cardholder for the purposes of that card's bonus restrictions. In other words, you can still apply for your own version of that card and earn its welcome bonus.

However, an authorized-user account may appear on your credit report and increase your 5/24 count.

If you're denied because of an authorized-user account, you may be able to explain the situation to Chase by calling the reconsideration line, although approval isn't guaranteed.

If you're interested in both a personal and business United card, applying for the business card first often makes sense. That's because the business card won't add to your 5/24 limit and tip you over the edge.

However, if you're applying for multiple personal United cards, the order you apply shouldn't matter. Pick whichever card is your highest priority first, considering its benefits and how its current offer compares with past bonuses.

The best choice depends on how often you fly United and which benefits you'll actually use.

United's eligibility rules are friendly to new applicants.

For the Gateway, Explorer, Quest, United Business and United Club Business cards, you're in a strong position if you don't currently hold the exact card and haven't received its welcome bonus within the past 24 months, while the United Club card has a minor caveat that won't impact most applicants.

#6190. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6189. Aer Lingus to Introduce First Premium Economy Cabin

Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

The carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

“[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”

The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

The carrier will also roll out new Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

New interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Plans call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

All seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

#6188. Rescue Missions: The Untold History Of The Boeing 747's Unique 5th Engine Mounting

Picture a legendary widebody aircraft thundering down a runway with five massive powerplants bolted beneath its wings, where only four of them are burning fuel and generating thrust. It may seem like an engineering experiment or a futuristic testbed flight, but this was a real logistical lifeline used during the height of the classic jet age. When a commercial airliner suffered a catastrophic engine failure at a remote airport thousands of miles from home, operators did not wait weeks for maritime freight or transport charters; instead, they simply strapped a spare, fully assembled jet engine directly under the wing and flew it there themselves.

Such an extraordinary capability centered around the Boeing 747's unique fifth-engine mounting system, an engineering marvel designed to rescue stranded airframes when conventional global supply chains failed. Why did Boeing incorporate a dedicated structural hardpoint specifically for hauling dead-weight turbofans across oceans, and how did flight crews manage the immense aerodynamic penalties of a multi-ton pod?

When the 747 entered commercial service in 1970, early high-bypass turbofans like the Pratt & Whitney JT9D and Rolls-Royce RB211 were revolutionary in fuel efficiency but notoriously temperamental compared to today's powerplants. If a widebody suffered a catastrophic engine failure at a remote international outstation, such as a distant hub in Asia, Africa, or the Middle East, airlines were met with a huge logistical problem. Standard cargo aircraft of the era frequently lacked the main-deck cargo door dimensions or payload capacity needed to transport a fully assembled, multi-ton turbofan core across continents.

The incompatibility created crippling Aircraft on Ground (AOG) delays that could strand a flagship aircraft out of service for weeks while awaiting maritime shipping or rare charter flights. To overcome this vulnerability, aviation pioneers drew upon operational precedents established during the dawn of the jet age. Analysis from Simple Flying notes that as early as 1959, Qantas began outfitting its Boeing 707 fleet with external mounting hardware to ferry replacement powerplants across international networks, a resourceful practice later adopted by operators of the Douglas DC-8 as well.

Recognizing that the much larger 747 would encounter identical outstation risks on expanding global routes, Boeing engineered a permanent solution directly into the aircraft's baseline wing architecture. They did so by building a dedicated hardpoint into the port wing so that the Queen of the Skies could act as its own heavy-lift delivery truck.

Mechanically, the fifth-pod system was based on a precision-engineered hardpoint located exclusively on the port wing, positioned inboard between the fuselage and the number two engine pylon. This location was deliberately chosen because it placed the massive secondary weight close to the aircraft centerline, minimizing structural stress on the outer wing spars. Technicians secured the replacement powerplant to a dummy strut designed to withstand extreme shear loads during takeoff, cruise, and landing without distorting the wing's aerodynamic profile.

Unlike the aircraft's active operating engines, the fifth-pod unit was entirely non-functional and carried purely as dead-weight freight. It featured zero plumbing, no fuel feed lines, no electrical wiring, and no hydraulic connections, meaning it contributed nothing to forward propulsion.

In order to prevent catastrophic windmilling and structural bearing damage from oncoming airflow, ground crews removed the forward fan blades or locked them securely, wrapping the core in streamlined aerodynamic fairings and nose-cone caps.

Positioning the multi-ton spare engine close to the fuselage root, engineers minimized dangerous center-of-gravity shifts that could compromise aircraft stability. Despite that, even with the weight efficiently distributed, strapping an exposed turbofan shell under one wing created a significant amount of parasitic drag that massively altered the aircraft's aerodynamic balance.

The aircraft remains one of the most unique aircraft in commercial aviation history.

When an unpowered turbofan is slung beneath the port wing, the resulting parasitic drag creates a persistent yawing tendency that flight crews must actively manage from takeoff to touchdown. The fifth pod sits exclusively on the left side, so the aircraft naturally wants to pull to the left, needing constant rudder deflection and precise trim adjustments to maintain coordinated flight. The reality was that even though the sheer mass of the airframe dealt with much of the disturbance, the asymmetric resistance needed unyielding pilot attention during initial climb phases and crosswind approaches.

To keep the aircraft flying straight and level within safe structural envelopes, flight manuals mandated strict operational limitations, including a maximum cruise speed reduction to around Mach 0.78 or lower to prevent aerodynamic buffeting around the mounting pylon, as noted in discussions from PPRuNe. Furthermore, the added weight of roughly 13,228 lb (6,000 kg) combined with increased drag penalized fuel consumption by 10% to 15%, slashing normal range capabilities.

For multi-thousand-mile rescue operations, this heavy fuel burn resulted in using strategic refueling stops, such as touching down at Perth Airport (PER) before attempting the long Indian Ocean crossing to Johannesburg, as noted in Qantas newsroom breakdowns.

The huge operational penalty made many of these standard delivery routes become carefully choreographed logistical hurdles, which not every airline ended up being able to manage. So which global airlines actually mastered this intricate procedure, and how did they complete the most famous rescue missions of the classic jet era?

The technical and aerodynamic penalties were, of course, formidable, though only a select group of international legacy operators mastered the fifth-pod procedure. During the classic widebody era of the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, airlines such as British Airways, Singapore Airlines, South African Airways, Aer Lingus, and Trans World Airlines kept certified engineering protocols to haul spare engines across their far-flung networks. Among these operators, Qantas emerged as the absolute master of the craft, making use of its geographical isolation at the bottom of the world to perfect fifth-pod logistics across decades of 707 and 747 operations.

The defining modern case study of this capability occurred on January 6, 2016, when Qantas deployed Boeing 747-438 registration VH-OJS on flight QF63 from Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) to Johannesburg O.R. Tambo International Airport (JNB). Making a crucial technical refueling stop at Perth Airport (PER), the aircraft carried a massive Rolls-Royce RB211 turbofan tucked beneath its port wing to rescue a grounded sister aircraft, registration VH-OJU, which was stranded without heavy maintenance support in South Africa. The meticulous operation skipped weeks of complex maritime shipping and unavailable cargo freighter charters, demonstrating the unmatched operational agility of a passenger jet acting as its own heavy-lift supply truck.

Even as flight QF63 proved that an airline could successfully rescue a stranded widebody using its own passenger fleet, the global aviation landscape was undergoing a transformation in the background. We no longer see these engine ferry flights, mainly because newer aircraft were never designed with the ability to attach an engine like this, so why is that the case?

The iconic passenger aircraft has been given a second lease of life.

The decline of the fifth-engine ferry system is a direct testament to the extraordinary reliability of modern aviation powerplants. In the 1970s, early turbofans experienced frequent mechanical hurdles that necessitated self-rescue solutions at remote international outstations. Today, advanced high-bypass turbofans achieve dispatch reliability rates exceeding 99.9%, as detailed in Simple Flying analysis, making mid-route engine failures at isolated hubs vanishingly rare and shifting airline operational risk profiles entirely.

Furthermore, the globalization of heavy air cargo networks ended the logistical necessity of external wing transport. Purpose-built super-transporters and modern nose-loading freighters, such as the Boeing 747-8F and the Antonov An-124, can easily accommodate fully assembled fan cases and engine cores within their main cargo decks.

It is also vital to distinguish these utilitarian cargo ferry pods from dedicated engine testbed aircraft, such as Pratt & Whitney's famous Boeing 747SP testbeds, which mount active powerplants on the forward fuselage or tail for in-flight engineering trials rather than commercial cargo transport.

Eventually, twin-engine widebodies came to dominate global long-haul routes and passenger 747s faded into retirement, and so the underwing hardpoints vanished from active airline fleets. Now that modern aviation looks toward ultra-long-range point-to-point networks, how will operators handle rare logistical emergencies when support is thousands of miles away?

The disappearance of the fifth-pod capability is really showing the end of an era when long-haul flight operations required sheer mechanical improvisation. When an aircraft could strap a six-tonne jet engine beneath its wing and power across oceans to rescue a stranded sister ship, it demonstrated an aviation philosophy built on frontline self-reliance. Today, that raw frontier spirit has been supplanted by predictive maintenance algorithms, digital supply chain tracking, and global logistics networks that move parts faster than any passenger flight ever could.

With passenger 747-400s being phased out of commercial service among operators, and modern twinjets like the A350 and 777X lacking any structural provision for external wing cargo, the hardpoints that once defined jumbo jet versatility exist now only in aviation museums and archival photographs. Comparing and contrasting this era and the current era of modern engine manufacturing really shows how far safety and design excellence has come, and leaves us wondering where the industry may head next.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6187. 14 tricks to getting the most value from your cruise vacations

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

Melinda Crow is a Texas-based freelance writer and guidebook author. From camping to cruising, she's been writing about travel for 30-plus years. Her first cruise was on Carnival’s second ship, Carnivale. She prefers shore excursions involving history, wine or wildlife.

Squeezing the most value out of every dollar on a cruise is a top goal for most travelers. It doesn't matter if you're on a quick escape cruise from a local port or an exotic luxury cruise halfway around the globe, you never want to end it feeling like you should have gotten more for your money.

Cruises are the ultimate all-inclusive vacation, with meals, transportation and entertainment included, and there is even more value-adds on board that you may have never thought to look for. The trick is to hone in on built-in value early, in the cruise shopping and purchasing stage, and then pay attention to every detail that might enhance your experience along the way. Here are 14 tricks to get the most possible value from any cruise you take.

It can feel like you’re bombarded with emails after you book a cruise, but some of them contain hidden treasure.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Princess, MSC and Virgin Voyages are among the cruise lines that use a bidding process to manage unsold cabins as the sailing date gets closer. Carnival Cruise Line offers upgrades without bidding. Pay attention to your email, and you might nab a nicer cabin for less than you’d pay by booking it outright.

Emails also alert you to discounted packages or bundles for Wi-Fi, shore excursions, specialty dining, drinks and even spa treatments. Much of the same information can be found on the cruise planner on the cruise line's website, but unless you log in often, watch those emails for value-oriented offers.

While it's tempting to always look at the newest (and often the biggest) ships, you may find that switching to an older or smaller ship, which may be just slightly less in demand, often helps squeeze more from your cruise budget without limiting your vacation fun.

You can also save hundreds of dollars by opting for inside staterooms, rooms with partially blocked views or those with less-than-perfect locations on the ship. This even works within suite zones or exclusive ship-within-a-ship areas. My dermatologist recently confided that he always chooses an inside suite within the Yacht Club when he cruises with MSC; he gets all the VIP perks, including exclusive dining and entertainment venues, for thousands less than the suites with balconies.

And don't rule out the cruise cabin guarantee option. Regardless of the cabin type, allowing the cruise line to select your stateroom is almost always the better value option than picking a specific room.

While most lines sign you up for loyalty programs automatically after your first sailing, you might need to opt in. Some lines allow you to sign up even before your first cruise, giving you advance offers to entice you to go ahead and book that first cruise.

Status matches between cruise lines are a huge bonus. MSC offers a status match with other cruise lines, hotel brands and tour operators. You can do this before your first booking and get Voyagers Club benefits on your first cruise with the line. These could be as simple as a welcome beverage or as elaborate as a complimentary tasting menu dinner. Ultra-luxury sister brand, Explora Journeys, offers a one-time status match with MSC and comparable luxury lines.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea have an ongoing status match across the three sister brands. That means you can reap rewards on a luxury line by earning status on a mainstream brand.

Similarly, Viking’s loyalty program spans its river, ocean and expedition arms. Once you’ve cruised with the line, you’ll get benefits fleetwide, even if you try out a different kind of ship.

Some lines offer casino status matches with land- and sea-based casinos that might even earn you a free cruise. These often come with exceptions; your casino status on Carnival won't get you a free cruise on sister line Princess, but casino status on Celebrity might. And don't be afraid of free cruise certificates handed out by reputable casinos on land where you have status. They’re the real deal, often based on long-standing partnerships between the casino and cruise lines. The reverse is also true. I’ve never been to WinStar Casino in Oklahoma, but they send me offers of free hotel nights using postcards featuring the Carnival logo, with which I have casino status.

While not every loyalty perk holds a huge value for you, little freebies definitely add up on vacation. For example, Carnival gives you a free 1.5-liter bottle of water on your second cruise. That's one less bottle you might have to buy.

As you move up the loyalty ladder, cruise by cruise, the perks improve. For example, you may be eligible for free laundry, drinks and specialty dining the higher up you go. I once met a couple who were on a five-night Royal Caribbean cruise for the sole purpose of moving up to the top loyalty tier before going on a much longer cruise. The higher tier would give them free Wi-Fi and a handful of other valuable perks for the duration of their longer cruise.

Often the onboard perks are loaded on your cabin keycard, but you might have to ask how to use them. For example, if you are entitled to a free bag of laundry at your loyalty level, nobody will hand you a bag and say, "Fill it up; it's free." It's up to you to know the perks you are entitled to and follow through on getting them.

Amid the barrage of marketing messages for beverage packages of all sorts, it's easy to forget that certain beverages are included in your cruise fare.

Every cruise ship offers standard drip coffee, water, iced tea, hot cocoa, punch or lemonade and a variety of tea bags free of charge. Milk and juice are available at breakfast. Look for self-serve stations at the buffet, or ask your server.

Sodas are included on premium lines like Windstar, Oceania and Viking, as well as on luxury lines like Seabourn, Silversea and Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Disney Cruise Line also offers free soft drinks but only from the beverage dispensers by the pool.

It's surprising how many free (or included) alcoholic drinks you can procure once on board a ship. I've been offered sparkling wine at art auctions, galley tours and captain's events.

Royal Caribbean and Celebrity both have free drinks for the top three tiers of loyalty status.

Celebrity Cruises offers free drinks for anyone gambling in the casino. Carnival and Virgin Voyages are among the lines offering free drinks to select gamblers based on their prior gambling history. You might be eligible for those, even if you only gamble on land.

The cabin you book might come with valuable perks, so know what they are so you don’t miss out.

For example, Celebrity’s AquaClass cabins come with not only thermal suite access and exclusive dining in the line’s health-forward restaurant called Blu, but also a choice of exercise equipment. Yoga mats are supposed to be in the closet when you board, but you'll have to ask for any of the other items listed on the menu provided.

Suites on most lines come with extra perks like included drink packages and specialty dining. On certain ships, even some smaller suite categories come with exclusive dining rooms only for the occupants of those categories. The food in these exclusive eateries is often a step above the main dining room and not to be missed if you are staying in the entitled category.

The same goes for suite lounge access. You generally find snack and beverage stations stocked with specialty treats you won’t find elsewhere on board, making it worthwhile to at least sneak a peek at the lounge offerings if you paid for a category that comes with access.

The cost of going out to the movies these days makes a cruise movie night a big value. Now that most of us watch movies by streaming them at home, actually going to the movies is a treat in and of itself.

Movie nights on a ship are a step above your local movie theater. You might enjoy films on a giant poolside screen while you float in the pool or relax on a lounge chair with bar servers bringing the drinks to you. Disney Cruise Line screens first-run films for free, with costumed characters in attendance. Many lines serve free popcorn wherever movies are being shown.

If staying in for a movie night in your jammies sounds good, take advantage of free or pay-per-view movies on your cabin’s TV. Disney is among the cruise lines with popcorn on the room service menu. On a Silversea cruise, I once told our butler we were staying in for an evening movie. His immediate reply was, "Shall I pop some corn for you?" The answer, of course, was, "Yes, please."

Live music, comedy acts, magic shows and musical theater are luxuries you can pay dearly for on land — but all of those are available on cruise lines at no charge. The larger the ship, the more entertainment options you will have.

Free live music is found daily in lounges, pool areas, atriums and on stage in the main auditorium. Audience participation game shows, sometimes raucous in nature, usually take over lounge space a few nights of the cruise.

The main stage will have a show nightly, either song-and-dance revues featuring an onboard cast or guest magicians, musicians and comedians, some with TV credits to their name. Larger ships might have separate comedy club venues to keep the laughs flowing every night of the cruise, with both family-friendly and adults-only shows. Clubs on dry land where these same performers appear often charge a $30-40 cover. On a recent Carnival cruise, I estimate my visits to the comedy club alone would have cost me several hundred dollars.

Some lines lean heavily into specialty performances. Look for ice skating, aquatic high-diving and dance shows on select Royal Caribbean ships and acrobatic performances on Virgin Voyages and MSC Cruises. Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line both offer Broadway musicals, while Disney produces live musical performances based on its popular animated movies.

With so much free entertainment that would certainly cost a family hundreds in ticket prices on land, you’ll get a ton of value from your cruise if you attend the shows that most appeal to you.

When the night's entertainment winds down, it's time to dance the night away and go clubbing — and cruise ship clubs don’t have a cover. Big ships crank up the party vibe after the last show in the main theater, so you can make the most of every second you’re awake. Hop from dance parties on the pool deck to karaoke in smaller bar venues and even silent discos in the atrium to keep the fun going into the wee hours.

Eating out and trying local restaurants are hallmarks of vacation, but you can blow your budget doing that on land. You can spend a lot on specialty restaurants on board, too, but pay attention to timing to get the most value out of the free dining on board. If you know you would enjoy steak and lobster, do a little research to figure out which night they will be served in the main dining room. You don’t want to find out too late that you booked a specialty restaurant on the same night you could have been eating surf and turf at no additional cost. Themed brunches and afternoon tea are also main dining room events you don’t want to miss.

Looking beyond the buffet and main dining room might turn up surprising food choices you didn't even know were included in your cruise fare. Pool grills serving juicy hamburgers, specialty coffee shops with snacks and even sandwiches and healthy choice salads near the solarium are all yummy examples of freebies tucked away in spots you might not think to look.

As for the specialty restaurants, those are generally still a bargain compared to a similar meal at a land-based restaurant. Carnival's Steakhouse is a good example. The cost is $52 per person. That sounds steep, but if you've priced a filet mignon in a nice restaurant lately, you'll know that $52 barely covers the steak. At Fahrenheit 555, you'll be treated to appetizers, sides and desserts, making the cover charge a vacation value. Book your Steakhouse dinner for the first night of a sailing, and Carnival will usually throw in a complimentary bottle of house wine.

For lounging in your cabin, free or low-cost room service boosts your cruise value. My personal favorite (especially on sea days) is enjoying a "first breakfast" of coffee and croissants from room service before heading out for a more substantial second breakfast.

Private island experiences provide an inexpensive break from paying for excursions in other ports. First things first, the beach is free. Use of the lounge chairs is free (not always the case at some vacation destinations). Swimming in the ocean and in some pools is free.

Depending on the island, you might find hammocks, hiking trails, game and sports areas and interesting snorkeling spots. Rental equipment for snorkeling and other water activities is usually reasonably priced, but you can bring your own gear.

The major private islands all have complimentary barbecue buffets and occasionally other food trucks or fast-casual offerings. As with specialty dining on the ship, even the up-charged food won’t cost as much as at a theme park or on the beach at a vacation destination.

Relying on shore excursions offered by the cruise line is the easy way to plan your days in port. It also keeps you safe from becoming one of those pier-running late-comers at departure time. Those tours are not always the best value, however. Lower-priced reputable port tours may take a bit more research on your part, but can save hundreds of dollars.

I recently enjoyed a 4-hour kayak tour in Ketchikan with pickup near the pier and guaranteed on-time return that I booked directly on the Ketchikan Kayak Company's website, which saved me roughly $60 per person compared to the similar tour offered by the ship.

And don’t forget that skipping organized tours altogether can also net you an amazing day in port. If tours aren't your jam, or you just don’t want the scheduling hassle in every port, consider simply venturing out on your own in search of fun. If the town is walkable, start with that. Or consider renting a car or simply hiring a taxi driver. I've visited Cozumel dozens of times on cruise ships, but had never seen the far side of the island. Last fall, a group of friends and family rented two Jeeps online from a rental agency located walking distance from the pier. We had a marvelous time stopping wherever we wanted, including for an impromptu tequila tasting (for the non-drivers, of course).

Whether you're talking about something as simple as miniature golf, basketball, pickleball or table tennis, or as elaborate as surf simulators and multideck dry slides, cruise lines often load their ships’ upper decks with free fun. As with all things on a cruise, certain activities come with a cost, but you’ll find plenty of fun that does not add to your cruise bill.

On land, you typically need to pay to access waterslides, splash parks, rock climbing walls and adventure and zip lines, but on many cruises, these active onboard attractions come free. Certain activities might require reservations or specific attire (like closed-toe shoes), so check out the details in advance.

Did you know that some cruise lines let you buy VIP packages pre-cruise for a bundle of preferential treatment similar to suite category perks? The real value of these programs lies in not paying for an expensive suite while enjoying extra perks as if you did.

Royal Caribbean's The Key includes early boarding times, a welcome lunch, fast lane access to select onboard activities, premium theater seating, departure day perks and free internet access for each guest who purchases the package.

Celebrity's Premium Access is a similar bundle. The combination of complimentary room service and Premium Wi-Fi for two devices makes this package a cruise value.

Holland America's Club Orange includes a complimentary cabin upgrade when available, priority check-in, priority lines at Guest Services and Shore Excursion desks, bathrobes, an expanded room service menu, a complimentary glass of sparkling wine, exclusive events like behind-the-scenes tours and coffee chats with performers and even separate dining rooms on some ships. With a bit of strategy, the cabin upgrade alone can justify the cost of the Club Orange add-on. This works best in Oceanview and Verandah categories where you can choose an obstructed view cabin at a low cost, banking on the Club Orange upgrade to a full-view room.

Carnival’s Faster to the Fun offers early cabin access, express luggage delivery and priority check-in and embarkation, shuttle boarding, dining reservations, Guest Services line and debarkation. Note that Carnival blocks access to FTTF for some loyalty guests, including some casino loyalty members, to avoid stacking of perks.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Priority Access includes priority security, check-in and boarding processes on embarkation day, plus skip-the-line tendering and debarkation, complimentary standard room service and a $50 spa discount on port days.

Cruises come with so much value bundled into the cost of the fare that it can be easy to overlook all the goodies that aren't costing you anything extra. Adding value to your cruise vacation can be as simple as reading the daily planner or taking a walk around the ship to discover all the included attractions. Whether it’s free entertainment in your favorite lounge, a dance lesson or no-cost prime rib in the main dining room, all those onboard freebies and low-cost add-ons make it possible to get outsize value from your cruise vacation.
