#6186. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6185. Would Alaska-Hawaiian 12-Year Widebody Captains Really Earn $493.41 An Hour Under The Tentative Pilot Contract?

Tada Images | Shutterstock, Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying

After more than 600 days of negotiations, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines came to a tentative Joint Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Air Line Pilots Association International (ALPA). The terms now dictate that a 12-year widebody captain will earn an eye-popping base rate of $493.41 an hour starting in early 2027. Most mainline airline pilots credit between 800 and 1,000 flight hours per year, meaning a $493.41 rate translates to roughly $395,000 to $493,000 in base flight pay.

That rate is only the starting point for 2027 and is scheduled to rise annually, reaching $539.16 per hour by 2030, according to Aero Crew News. The Black Box Aviation Podcast reported that rates will be adjusted annually to match the average of American, Delta, Southwest, and United on comparable aircraft, or increase by at least 3%, whichever is greater. Alaska Air Group will also contribute 18% directly to 401(k) accounts, alongside a performance-based program with 5% annual payouts.

The terms ALPA agreed to on November 10 will be put to a vote on December 1 for the 4,600 union membersto collectively ratify, according to Airline Geeks. If approved, the new pay scales take effect on January 31, 2027. The new contract represents an immediate raise from $86.41 to $102.41 per hour, or a 21.2% to 26.2% pay bump.

The agreement is a long-awaited resolution following Alaska Air Group’s $1.9 billion acquisition of Hawaiian in September 2024. While the Federal Aviation Administration approved the financial merger and granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, aircrews remained divided. Formal joint negotiations launched in February 2025, aiming not only to set uniform pay rates but also to establish an operational framework to reorganize the pilots and jets of the combined fleet.

ALPA negotiators built the new agreement on Alaska’s existing contract framework while preserving legacy Hawaiian protections. Until the unified labor contract is official, management cannot freely assign pilots across both of the newly combined networks or readily swap aircraft to new airfields based on changing demand.

Captain Drew Coyle, the Alaska Airlines MEC chair, commented on the negotiations.

“Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex issues facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”

The tentative agreement also clears a major labor hurdle to Alaska’s long-haul expansion and Hawaiian's $600 million modernization plan. Alaska is expecting up to 17 new Boeing 787 Dreamliners that will launch 12 new overseas routes. Meanwhile, Hawaiian’s fleet overhaul in Honolulu will retrofit all 24 Airbus A330-200 widebodies with new Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Still, flying two dozen midlife A330s alongside new 787s forces the airline to maintain separate supply chains, training programs, and maintenance programs.

Passing this contract is only half the battle because Alaska and Hawaiian pilots still cannot fly each other's jets until their seniority lists merge. Under federal law, a neutral arbitrator must combine both pilot rosters into a single master list. Because seniority controls everything from captain upgrades to holiday schedules, pilots must stay separated on their legacy fleets until that process finishes.

Before seniority talks even wrap up, all 4,600 member pilots must approve the four-year agreement itself. Union voting runs from December 1 through December 22. If a majority votes yes, the new pay rates and scheduling rules officially take effect on January 31, 2027, locking in labor stability through January 30, 2031, while eliminating the old pay gap between both workforces.

Captain Larry Payne, the Hawaiian Airlines MEC chair, also remarked on the agreement.

“This joint collective bargaining agreement represents an important milestone for both pilot groups. The decisions made throughout these negotiations will shape our pilots’ careers and quality of life for years to come. If approved, this agreement will establish the foundation for future contracts as we move forward together as one pilot group.”

Once seniority lists finally combine, Alaska Air Group can unleash the full scheduling flexibility it bought with the merger. Management will be able to shift crews seamlessly between Hawaii's refreshed narrowbodies and Seattle's growing Dreamliner fleet as seasonal travel shifts. That operational freedom was impossible after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, merging safety rules but leaving cockpits divided.

Ultimately, locking in $493.41 an hour for widebody captains proves Alaska is serious about competing alongside major legacy airlines on global routes. Yet paying top-tier wages across both fleets raises the stakes for every flight across the Pacific. The carrier's long-term financial success now hinges on whether it can fill those upgraded cabins at profitable fares against tough domestic and international rivals.

Executives cite disproportionate overhead and geopolitical fuel shocks as they realign post merger operations and roles.

As part of the merger, Alaska took over Hawaiian's 787 Dreamliner orders and rebranded its existing 787s to construct an international gateway at its historic Seattle-Tacoma International (SEA) base. To make the increased $493.41 widebody pay rate financially viable, Alaska is dividing its twin-aisle jets across the combined fleet's two unique hubs. Thus, Hawaiian maintains its legacy A330-200s in Honolulu to meet established island leisure and regional Pacific demand.

Hawaiian originally sought the 787-9 in 2018 to upgrade its fleet and increase capacity on long-haul Pacific routes. Hawaiian even canceled a prior order for six A330neos because the Dreamliner had superior fuel efficiency, longer range, and more business-class seating in densely populated markets such as Tokyo and New York. Hawaiian eventually increased its commitment to 12 Dreamliners before merging with Alaska.

Alaska now has widebody jets, experienced pilots, and foreign operating certificates, which it lacked as a primarily narrowbody airline before acquiring Hawaiian. From Seattle, Alaska deploys the 787-9 on ultra-long, high-demand routes to Tokyo Narita, Seoul, London, Rome, Paris, and Athens. The Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency are an ideal fit for these business and luxury travel corridors where higher ticket prices offset premium pilot wages.

In January, Alaska placed a historic order for 105 737 MAX 10s and five more 787-10s, pushing its total Boeing order book past 240 planes. This international push fits naturally with the airline's identity as a fiercely loyal, all-Boeing mainline operator based in Boeing’s backyard. By folding Hawaiian’s Dreamliners into an all-Boeing fleet, Alaska avoids the high cost of training crews and stocking parts for Airbus widebodies.

Back in Honolulu, Hawaiian’s A330-200 fleet anchors core flights to Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, Sydney, Papeete, and Pago Pago, alongside major West Coast cities. Starting in 2028, Hawaiian will upgrade all 24 jets with new Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Although older A330s lack the Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency, their lower ownership costs bring costs down to make economy vacation airfare more affordable.

Apart from this change, today will also see the airline finally join Alaska Airlines in the oneworld alliance.

The narrowbody crews of the combined Alaska-Hawaiian fleet are about to undergo a significant fleet makeover, much like the widebody pilots who fly long ocean trips. Hawaiian is retiring its outdated 717s, which are frequently used for interisland flights between Honolulu and nearby islands. As part of the expanded narrowbody business in the continental US, Alaska Air Group is moving some 737-800s to Hawaii and bringing its own new 737 MAX 8 and MAX 10 aircraft.

Under the new deal, 12-year narrowbody captains are paid $401.09 per hour. That's $92.32 less than widebody captains. Despite the lower hourly pay, narrowbody pilots perform significantly more takeoffs and landings every shift. This is especially true for crews doing 30-minute island hops. Replacing the 128-seat 717 with larger 737s will add dozens of additional seats per flight while also updating the flight deck, saving fuel on each sortie, and decreasing fleet maintenance. The pilots will have to train on a larger airframe, but the airline will be able to transport more passengers without recruiting additional workers.

Switching to an all-737 narrowbody fleet simplifies pilot training and spare parts across both airlines. Instead of maintaining separate cockpit ratings for 717s, A321neos, and 737s, pilots can eventually fly a single narrowbody type across West Coast and island routes. This standardization lets management smoothly shift crews between mainland and island flying whenever seasonal travel demand spikes or dips.

Still, operating larger 737s on short interisland routes brings clear economic and mechanical trade-offs. Because the 737-800 is much heavier than the 717, it burns more fuel per trip and puts extra wear on brakes and landing gear during frequent landings. However, the higher seat capacity lowers the cost per passenger, helping the airline offset those added baseline expenses.

#6184. American to Renovate, Expand Phoenix Lounges

American Airlines plans to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a new servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

Longer-term plans call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a new self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

“Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden said in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”

The planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.

#6183. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new route to Washington, D.C., next year.

#6181. JetBlue Doubles Down In Fort Lauderdale With New Flights To Grand Cayman & Honduras In 2027

JetBlue Airways announced two new daily international services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) on Thursday, connecting South Florida with Grand Cayman and Tegucigalpa in Honduras starting in February 2027. The airline says its latest move will expand its international network at the airport to 20 destinations, strengthening its position as a gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean.

These latest additions follow Spirit Airlines' collapse in May, which created substantial opportunities at its former Fort Lauderdale stronghold. JetBlue has moved aggressively to capture displaced demand, with an analysis of Department of Transportation (DOT) data revealing that the airline's international passenger traffic is growing even faster than its added capacity.

The first new service will launch on February 23, connecting Fort Lauderdale with Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman. Two days later, JetBlue will begin flying to Palmerola International Airport (XPL) in Comayagua, serving the Honduran capital, Tegucigalpa. Both routes will operate daily using Airbus A220 and A320 family aircraft, with introductory one-way fares starting at $99 and $183, respectively.

The Honduras route will be JetBlue's first service to the Tegucigalpa area, complementing its existing San Pedro Sula operation. Daniel Shurz, JetBlue's Senior Vice President of Network Planning, emphasized the airline's commitment to expanding international connectivity and providing more options for travelers visiting friends and relatives.

"We're grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we're committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they're looking for. With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we're strengthening Fort Lauderdale's role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean."

Grand Cayman represents a return following JetBlue's short-lived service introduced in December 2025. The airline will also offer temporary daily flights to Port of Spain between January 29 and February 15 for Trinidad and Tobago's Carnival. Following the recent launch of new routes to Barranquilla and Cali, Colombia, JetBlue expects to exceed 150 daily departures at FLL during winter peaks, its largest schedule ever.

JetBlue's international expansion at Fort Lauderdale has been substantial. An analysis of DOT T-100 International Segment data (available through August) shows the airline offered almost 1.7 million international seats in the first eight months of this year, up 33.4% year-on-year. The growth reflects an increasingly diverse network, with new and restored routes complementing established Caribbean and Latin American services.

Much of the additional capacity stems from six international routes launched or restored in December 2025, including Aruba, Cartagena, Grand Cayman, Liberia, San Pedro Sula, and Sint Maarten. Meanwhile, Guayaquil, Guatemala City, and Santiago have also seen significant growth, showing how JetBlue has strengthened previously limited operations.

However, growth has not been uniform. Montego Bay experienced a 33.9% capacity reduction, while Kingston, Cancún, and Punta Cana also recorded declines. The expansion has also coincided with international route reductions elsewhere in its network. The net result is that JetBlue is not only growing its FLL international network but also diversifying it and concentrating capacity where opportunities are strongest.

JetBlue’s latest growth spurt cements its rise as Fort Lauderdale’s new number one airline.

Although JetBlue's international expansion at FLL was already underway before Spirit's demise on May 2, the vacuum left by its former competitor has given it the space to accelerate that growth. To assess performance after Spirit's exit, Simple Flying zoomed in on DOT T-100 data for May-August, compared with the same period last year.

The findings are striking. JetBlue has increased its international seat capacity by 33.0%, yet passenger traffic surged by 45.8%, lifting average load factors from 79.4% to 87.0%, an improvement of 7.6 percentage points. For context, Delta Air Lines averages about 85% load factors on its international routes, and at 87%, Fort Lauderdale is the top-performing base in JetBlue's network.

This clearly demonstrates that JetBlue has not yet reached the limits of demand at Fort Lauderdale, because even as it adds more capacity, it is attracting even more passengers and filling a greater proportion of those seats. And there is the knock-on effect: Growing international passenger volumes also increase ancillary revenues, with JetBlue reporting 20% year-on-year loyalty revenue growth in Q3 2026, alongside a 55% increase in co-branded credit card acquisitions in South Florida.

A larger international network will certainly reinforce those trends. However, the airline's longer-term success will depend on translating this rapid passenger growth into stronger yields and sustainable commercial returns.

Why we like it: This welcome offer includes a Global Companion Award, which knocks up to 25,000 points off a companion’s award ticket when you book two award seats on Alaska, Hawaiian or a partner airline (including Oneworld members)in any class. The card also offers an ongoing 25,000-point Global Companion Award after each card anniversary.

Cardholders can also earn a 100,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $60,000 or more in a card anniversary year.

For frequent international travelers, earning 3 points per dollar spent on foreign transaction purchases is a major advantage and can help quickly accrue Atmos Rewards points. Why we like it: The Ascent offers a lower-cost way to earn Atmos Rewards points while receiving practical airline benefits. For travelers who fly Alaska or Hawaiian a few times each year, the free checked-bag benefit and preferred boarding could help justify the $95 annual fee.

The welcome offer also includes a Companion Fare, which can provide additional value for travelers who regularly fly with someone else.

Small-business owners who fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines regularly the is worth considering. It underwent a refresh in Nov. 2026 and now offers new earning opportunities, additional travel perks and a flat annual fee that covers employee cards at no additional cost.

Welcome offer: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

The points in this bonus are worth $1,440, per TPG's valuations. Unlike the personal cards, this represents the highest points offer we've ever seen on the card.

Annual fee: $195 per company (with free employee cards)

The refreshed card no longer includes the annual $99 Companion Fare or the $100 Alaska Lounge+ membership discount. Existing cardholders will retain their current benefits and won't automatically transition to the new version.

Why we like it: The 10-point earning rate is a standout benefit for businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian Airlines, representing a 16% return on eligible flights booked through Atmos for Business based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Free employee cards extend perks like checked bags and preferred boarding to more travelers, while four annual lounge passes and waived same-day change fees add value for the primary cardholder. Together, these benefits make the card particularly appealing to businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Business.

The Atmos Rewards cards are offering bonuses that allow new cardholders to add a haul of points to their accounts.

#6178. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6177. What Air Force One Pilots Do Before Flights That Most Other Pilots Never Do

Standard actions for a commercial airline crew before a flight include reviewing the flight with each other, followed by a pre-flight walkaround. Later, the crew sets up the flight deck, inputs their flight plan into the aircraft's computer, and verifies the aircraft's weight and balance figures before pushback. It's a thorough procedure to ensure the aircraft is fully ready to operate safely, and these procedures apply to essentially every commercial flight.

The pilots of Air Force One also do these actions, but their pre-flight duties are much more thorough because of their job: transporting the President of the United States. Air Force One is a callsign used to denote any US Air Force (USAF) aircraft flying the President, but it is most commonly associated with two Boeing VC-25As and the VC-25B Bridge, which are based on the Boeing 747. Crucially, the flight crew is concerned not just with safety, but also with security.

The two VC-25As are typically flown by two pilots, a flight engineer, and a navigator, while the VC-25B Bridge does not require a flight engineer (because it's based on the newer 747-8). Before each flight, they coordinate with ground crews to verify that the apron and runway are clear of potential debris. The flight plan itself may look significantly different from what airliners operate, and the crew also needs to ensure that the aircraft's onboard security and defense systems are operational.

In addition to these actions, the flight crew of Air Force One needs to help maintain security. This means not just coordinating with security teams on the apron, but also with air traffic control to ensure that the airport and surrounding airspace is clear of any potential conflicts. The crew also verifies that the aircraft will receive priority handling from air traffic control, and they also must review aerial refueling procedures for the VC-25A, although this capability has never been used with the president onboard.

The pilots typically must arrive three to four hours before the scheduled flight, coordinating with the US Secret Service to maintain security on the aircraft and at the airport. The aircraft is inspected, and its systems are tested to check for any potential technical faults. In addition, the crew has to review emergency procedures while also performing the more typical actions that you'd expect during the pre-flight flow. While this is usually a multi-hour process, flight crews are trained to perform departures with as little as an hour's notice.

Every long-distance trip undertaken by the US president begins and ends at the White House South Lawn. Here, the president boards a US Marine Corps helicopter operating under the callsign 'Marine One', the callsign used for any USMC aircraft carrying the US president. The helicopter, which may be joined by several others during the trip, flies to Andrews Air Force Base, home to the Presidential Airlift Group. The flight typically takes about six to ten minutes, and when the president lands, Air Force One is already waiting.

The VC-25s not only carry the president, but they also transport the president's Secret Service detail, senior staff, medical personnel, and advisors. In addition, the aircraft will typically carry the White House press pool, a rotating group of reporters and journalists covering the president. The president is always the last person to board the aircraft, and once he/she is onboard, the doors close before the engines are started. From there, the aircraft taxis to the runway and takes off.

Upon arrival, the airport receiving Air Force One typically suspends operations. From there, the president may either take a motorcade or another US Marine Corps helicopter to their final destination. The vehicles required for the motorcade and the USMC helicopters are typically flown in ahead of time via a Lockheed C-5 Galaxy to ensure that they're ready for the president's arrival. When it's time to return to Washington, this process repeats itself.

A former Air Force official claimed there wasn’t enough time to equip the aircraft with all of the “normal” modifications.

The pilots commanding the VC-25s must be experienced airmen serving with the US Air Force. Generally, these crew members have prior experience operating complex multi-engine transport aircraft and must have logged a significant number of flight hours (generally at least 2,500 hours). From there, pilots usually transfer to the 89th Airlift Wing at Andrews Air Force Base and build experience transporting other executives on aircraft like the Boeing C-32 or C-40 Clipper.

Pilots must maintain an exemplary flying record while serving in the USAF and keep a spotless permanent record. In addition, they must earn high-level qualifications to stand out further. Senior leadership evaluates the pilot roster at the 89th Airlift Wing, then handpicks the top aviators to enter the selection process for the Presidential Airlift Group. From there, the selection process includes interviews, psychological screenings, and simulator tests.

The final piece for those selected to pilot the VC-25 is to obtain 'Yankee White' clearance. This is a special, top-level security clearance reserved for personnel supporting the US president and vice president, and getting it requires an extremely thorough background check. Investigators may interview family members and peers, as well as former neighbors or teachers to verify stability, loyalty, and dependability, in a process that can take as long as a year. Candidates must also have a spotless criminal and financial history.

The VC-25As that commonly serve as Air Force One are designed to serve as invulnerable command centers in the sky. They feature advanced defense and communications systems, while also being equipped with aerial refueling systems so that they may remain airborne until food and water run out. However, the 747-based VC-25As are also massive aircraft. Not every airport can easily accommodate the VC-25As, and they draw a huge amount of attention, which isn't always ideal.

While the VC-25As are the most common aircraft that serve as Air Force One, the US president also occasionally travels on the Boeing C-32A, based on the 757-200. These planes are generally used when the president is traveling to airfields that cannot accommodate the VC-25A, and they can also be used as a backup aircraft when the president travels, as well as if a VC-25A is unavailable. Furthermore, the C-32s are useful when the president is traveling on sensitive missions, such as to active war zones.

In February 2023, former president Joe Biden secretly traveled to Ukraine, marking the first time in modern history that a US president had visited an active war zone not under the control of the US. To get there, he took a C-32A rather than the VC-25A, stopping at Ramstein Air Base in Germany for refueling before proceeding to Poland, where he boarded a train to Ukraine. The C-32 was preferable because of the sensitivity of the mission, and the flight didn't even use the standard Air Force One callsign in this case; rather, the callsign used was 'SAM060'.

A review of the differences between the older B747-200 vs the older VC-25A Air Force One (AFO). Then review the newer B747-8i vs the new VC-25B AFO.

The two VC-25As were delivered in the early 1990s and are based on the 747-200B, an aircraft that first entered service in the early 1970s. They're old and increasingly unreliable, and maintaining these aircraft is becoming difficult and expensive. As such, the USAF selected the 747-8 to serve as the platform for the replacement VC-25B in 2015, with first delivery scheduled for 2024. However, this has been pushed back multiple times, with first delivery now targeted for 2028.

In 2025, the US government accepted a 747-8 configured as a business jet from the Qatari government as a gift. This aircraft, now titled the VC25B Bridge, is intended to serve as an interim supplement for the existing VC-25A fleet until the two VC-25Bs are ready. The focus with the VC-25B Bridge was to get the aircraft ready as soon as possible, and it entered service in July 2026, less than a year after it was accepted. The catch is that it lacks many of the safety and defense features that are typically needed for the missions.

The VC-25B Bridge is only intended to be in service until the VC-25Bs arrive, and the aircraft is set to be retired before the end of President Donald Trump's second term. The VC-25Bs that will succeed it are conversions of whitetail aircraft, but they are being retrofitted with a full assortment of security, communications, and defensive technologies. Not only will they replace the VC-25B Bridge, but they will also replace the VC-25As, and they will be among the world's most advanced and secure aircraft in service.

#6175. Sunrise Airways Launches New U.S. Service

Haiti’s Sunrise Airways this week launched a new route to the U.S. Northeast.

The carrier on Tuesday operated its inaugural flight between Cap-Haïtien and New York-JFK. Flights will operate twice per week going forward.

Sunrise is one of only two airlines currently connecting the U.S. and Haiti. It also serves Boston, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Miami from Cap-Haïtien.

American Airlines resumed service to the country earlier this month after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by rising gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince. It is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haïtien.
